unit.title: Shapes and Symmetry
unit.blurb: Properties of quadrilaterals and regular polygons, the circumference of a circle, and 3D shapes: nets, plans and elevations.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Identify and describe the properties of quadrilaterals and regular polygons, including symmetry.

O2.t: Know and use the formula for the circumference of a circle.

O3.t: Use nets, plans and elevations of 3D shapes, and count faces, edges and vertices.

p: Square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, kite and trapezium are the special quadrilaterals. Describe them by their **sides**, **angles**, **diagonals** and **symmetry**.
A **parallelogram** has two pairs of parallel sides and rotational symmetry of order 2 but no lines of symmetry. A **kite** has one line of symmetry.
A **regular** polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal. A regular n-sided polygon has **n lines of symmetry** and **rotational symmetry of order n**.

lesson.t: Why the interior angles of a polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°
p: From one corner of an n-sided polygon you can draw diagonals that split it into n − 2 triangles. Each triangle gives 180°.

lesson.t: Diagonals are not always lines of symmetry
p: A rectangle's diagonals are NOT lines of symmetry: folding along one does not match the halves.

p: The **circumference** is the distance round a circle. The **diameter** goes across through the centre; the **radius** is half the diameter.
For every circle, circumference ÷ diameter is the same number, **π** (pi) ≈ 3.14159…  So **C = πd = 2πr**.

lesson.q: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 6 cm, to 1 decimal place.

p: For every circle, the circumference divided by the diameter is the same number, about 3.14. We call it π. So C = πd, or C = 2πr.
Try it: a lid with diameter 10 cm has a circumference of about 31.4 cm – a bit more than 3 diameters.
If you are given the radius, double it (or use 2πr). Using πr gives half the circumference.

p: A cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. A triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices. A square-based pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices.
For these shapes, **faces + vertices − edges = 2** (Euler's rule).
A **plan** is the view from above. A **front elevation** is the view from the front and a **side elevation** is the view from the side.
A cylinder's plan is a circle; its front elevation is a rectangle.
Hidden edges and faces still count. Use Euler's rule to check: F + V − E = 2.
